title: Auto Rides
description: Negotiate fares, give directions, and talk to auto drivers like a local

questions.prompt: You're at the roadside and want to know if the auto driver will go to Indiranagar. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Hoguttira? = will you go? (asking the driver). Hogidhe = I went (past tense, wrong). Baruttira? = will you come? (wrong direction).

questions.prompt: The auto driver says 'Meter-nalli hogona'. What does he mean?
questions.explanation: Meter-nalli = on meter. Hogona = let's go. A good sign — means they're willing to use the meter.

questions.prompt: You want to ask how much it costs to go to MG Road.
questions.explanation: Eshtu = how much. Aagutte = will it be / will it cost. MG Road-ge eshtu aagutte? = How much will it be to MG Road?

questions.prompt: The driver asks for 200 rupees but you think 150 is fair. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Kodi = give/make it. Saakaagatte = it will be enough / that's sufficient. 150 kodi, saakaagatte = make it 150, that'll do. Tumba jaasti = too much (also useful but less direct for bargaining).

questions.prompt: You offer 120 and the driver says 'Aagalla'. What does he mean?
questions.explanation: Aagalla = cannot / not possible / no. Aagutte = possible/OK. Illa = no. Aagalla is the key word for refusal.

questions.prompt: You want to say 'OK, let's go' after agreeing on a price. Complete: '___ hogona'
You're in the auto and say 'Nere hogi'. What are you telling the driver?
questions.explanation: Nere = straight. Hogi = go. Nere hogi = go straight. Essential for giving directions.

questions.prompt: You need the driver to turn left at the signal.
questions.explanation: Edakke = to the left. Balaakke = to the right. Tiri = turn. Signal-nalli edakke tiri = turn left at the signal.

questions.prompt: You've arrived at your destination. What do you say to stop the auto?
questions.explanation: Illi = here. Nilli = stop. Illi nilli = stop here. Hogi = go, Baa = come — wrong commands to stop.

questions.prompt: You say 'Aashte haadi-nalli balaakke tiri'. What do you mean?

options.text: Turn right on the eighth road
Go straight to the eighth road
The eighth road is to the left

questions.explanation: Aashte = eighth. Haadi = road/street. Balaakke = right. Tiri = turn. Haadi is the local word for a small road or lane.

questions.prompt: You want to say 'A little further ahead'.
questions.explanation: Swalpa = a little. Munde = ahead/forward. Hinde = behind/back. Swalpa munde hogi = go a little ahead.

questions.prompt: You want to say 'Stop near the tea shop'. Complete: 'Chai angadi ___ nilli'
The meter shows 85 rupees. The driver demands 120. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Nodri = look (respectful command). Meter nodri = look at the meter. Aagutte = it's/it'll be. Meter nodri, 85 aagutte = Look at the meter, it's 85.

questions.prompt: The driver says 'Chakra jaasti aagutte'. What is he complaining about?

options.text: Traffic was heavy / the detour cost more

questions.explanation: Chakra = traffic (literally 'circles'). Jaasti = more/extra. Aagutte = it becomes. He's saying traffic added to the cost.

questions.prompt: You want to say 'I only have a hundred rupees note'.
questions.explanation: Naange = to me / I have. noTu = note (currency). maatrame = only. ide = there is. 'I only have a 100 rupee note' is a very common auto negotiation phrase.

questions.prompt: You ask 'Chillare ide?' What are you asking?
questions.explanation: Chillare = change (coins/small notes). Ide? = is there? Chillare ide? = Do you have change? Crucial after every auto ride.

questions.prompt: The driver says he has no change and expects you to pay more. You want to say 'I'll pay exactly the meter amount'.
questions.explanation: Irostu = however much there is / the exact amount. Maatrame = only. Koduttene = I will give. 'I'll give only the meter amount' — a firm, fair response.

questions.prompt: To thank the driver and leave, you say 'Sari, ___'

title: At the Market
description: Buy vegetables, fruit, and groceries — bargain like a local

questions.prompt: You want to ask 'How much is one kilo of tomatoes?'
questions.explanation: Ondu = one. Kilo = kilogram. Eshtu = how much. This is the core market question — works for any vegetable.

questions.prompt: The vendor says 'Noorupayege eradu kilo'. What's the deal?
questions.explanation: Noorupaye = 100 rupees. Eradu = two. Kilo = kilo. Noorupayege eradu kilo = two kilos for 100 rupees. -ge suffix here means 'for (that price)'.

questions.prompt: You think 60 rupees per kilo is too expensive. What do you say?

options.text: Tumba jaasti aagutte, swalpa kammagi kodi

questions.explanation: Tumba jaasti = too much. Kammagi = less/cheaper. Kodi = give. Swalpa kammagi kodi = give a little cheaper. Classic bargaining phrase.

questions.prompt: The vendor says 'Chenna maal, rate fixed'. What is he telling you?
questions.explanation: Chenna = good/beautiful. Maal = goods/produce. Rate fixed = price is non-negotiable. He's defending the price with a quality claim.

questions.prompt: You want half a kilo of onions.
questions.explanation: Eerulli = onion. Ardha = half. Kodi = give (polite command). Eerulli ardha kilo kodi = give half a kilo of onions.

questions.prompt: You want to say 'Give me two of those'. Complete: 'Adhu ___ kodi'
The vendor quotes 80 rupees per kilo. You want to counter-offer with 60.
questions.explanation: Aruvattu = 60. Tagondi = take (respectful). Sari-aa = is it OK? Aruvattu rupaye tagondi, sari-aa? = Take 60 rupees, is that OK? Polite counter-offer.

questions.prompt: The vendor says 'Ninna rate-nalli hogalla, min 70'. What does he mean?

options.text: Can't go at your price, minimum 70

questions.explanation: Ninna = your. Rate-nalli = at that rate. Hogalla = won't go / can't do. Min = minimum. He's countering your offer with a floor price of 70.

questions.prompt: You've seen the same thing cheaper across the street. You want to say 'That shop gives it for less'.
questions.explanation: Aa = that. Angadi = shop. Nalli = in/at. Kammagi = cheaper/less. Koduttare = they give (third person plural). A classic move that often works.

questions.prompt: You've agreed on a price and want to buy two kilos. You say:
questions.explanation: Sari = OK. Eradu = two. Pakka maadi = pack it properly (respectful command). Pakka = packed/proper. Once agreed, this confirms the purchase.

questions.prompt: The vendor puts a bit extra on the scale and says 'Swalpa extra hakidde'. What did he do?

options.text: Added a little extra (as a gesture)

questions.explanation: Swalpa = a little. Extra = extra. Hakidde = I put/added. This is a common friendly vendor gesture — adding a little bonus. You can smile and say 'Dhanyavaada'.

questions.prompt: You want to ask 'Is it fresh?' Complete: 'Fresh ___ ide?'
questions.hint: aagide = is it / has it become (used to ask if something is fresh/ready)

questions.prompt: What does 'Bende kayi' mean?
questions.explanation: Bende kayi = okra/ladies finger. Kayi = vegetable/fruit (raw). Very common in Karnataka cuisine.

questions.prompt: You want to ask for 'a bunch of coriander'.
questions.explanation: Kottambri = coriander. Soppu = leafy greens. Kattu = bunch. Ondu kattu = one bunch. Soppu is the general word for leafy vegetables.

questions.prompt: The vendor gives you wilted coriander. You want to say 'Give me fresh ones'.
questions.explanation: Fresh-aagirostu = the ones that are fresh. Kodi = give. You can point and say this — the vendor will understand.

questions.prompt: The vendor holds up a bag of mixed vegetables and says 'Kootu tarkari'. What is it?
questions.explanation: Kootu = a dry Karnataka curry dish. Tarkari = vegetables. Kootu tarkari is a pre-mixed bag of vegetables perfect for making kootu — a common offering at Karnataka markets.

questions.prompt: You want to say 'I'll take this much' while pointing to a pile.
questions.explanation: Ishtu = this much (pointing). Tagondi = take/I'll take. Eshtu = how much (question). Idu beda = I don't want this.

questions.prompt: You're done shopping and want to say 'I don't need anything else'. Complete: 'Bere ___ beda'
questions.hint: enu = anything/nothing. Bere enu = anything else.

title: Tea Stall & Darshini
description: Order chai, coffee, and breakfast at local eateries

questions.prompt: You walk up to a tea stall. How do you order one cutting chai?
questions.explanation: Cutting = half-glass strong tea (local Bangalore slang). Ondu = one. Kodi = give. 'Ondu cutting kodi' is what locals say — no need to say 'chai'.

questions.prompt: The stall owner asks 'Sakkare haakali-aa?'. What does he want to know?
questions.explanation: Sakkare = sugar. Haakali = should I put/add? -aa = question marker. Sakkare haakali-aa? = Should I put sugar? Common question for tea orders.

questions.prompt: You want a filter coffee with less sugar.
questions.explanation: Swalpa = a little. Kamma = less. Sakkare = sugar. Swalpa kamma sakkare = a little less sugar. You can also just say 'kamma sakkare'.

questions.prompt: The owner brings your chai but it's lukewarm. You want to politely say 'It's not hot enough'.
questions.explanation: Swalpa bisi illa = a little not-hot / not hot enough. Bisi = hot. Illa = not/no. You can add 'maade kodi' (please heat it) but this softer phrase is less confrontational.

questions.prompt: The owner says 'Nimma chai ready aagutte, swalpa wait maadi'. What is he saying?

options.text: Your chai will be ready soon, wait a little
The chai is getting cold, drink quickly
We're out of chai, wait for next batch

questions.explanation: Nimma = your (formal). Ready aagutte = will be ready. Swalpa = a little. Wait maadi = please wait. Very common phrase at busy tea stalls.

questions.prompt: You want two teas. Complete: '___ cutting kodi'
You want to order two idlis and a vada.
questions.explanation: Eradu = two. Ondu = one. Kodi = give me. At a darshini you just list what you want and say kodi. Simple and effective.

questions.prompt: You want to know what breakfast items are available today. What do you ask?
questions.explanation: Enu enu = what what / what all. Ide = is there. Indu = today. Enu enu ide indu? = What all is there today? The casual doubling of 'enu' is very natural in spoken Kannada.

questions.prompt: The darshini guy says 'Khali plate-ge extra charge ide'. What does that mean?

options.text: There's an extra charge for empty plate (plate service)
The empty plate means they're out of food
Charging extra because the plate is large

questions.explanation: Khali = empty. Plate-ge = for the plate. Extra charge ide = there is an extra charge. Some darshinis charge separately for the plate/service — good to know upfront.

questions.prompt: The dosa isn't crispy enough. You want to say 'Make it a bit more crispy'.
questions.explanation: Swalpa jaasti = a little more. Crispy = crispy (borrowed word). Maadi kodi = please do/make. You can point to the tawa and say this — they'll understand.

questions.prompt: You've finished eating and want to ask for the bill.
questions.explanation: Bill kodi = give the bill. Simple and universally understood. No need to add anything else at a local darshini.

questions.prompt: You want extra chutney. Complete: 'Swalpa ___ kodi'
questions.hint: chutney is the same word in Kannada — and it's served free at darshinis!

questions.prompt: You're a regular. The chai wala greets you and asks 'Ninna haage?'. What is he asking?
questions.explanation: Ninna haage = same as last time / like yesterday. At a local stall, once you're a regular they'll remember your order. 'Ninna haage?' means 'the usual?'

questions.prompt: You want to say 'Yes, same as usual'.
questions.explanation: Howdu = yes. Ninna haagene = exactly like before / same as usual. Adding 'ne' emphasizes 'same.' A great phrase for regulars.

questions.prompt: You tell the chai wala 'Indu tumba busy'. What are you saying?

options.text: The tea is very strong today

questions.explanation: Indu = today. Tumba = very/a lot. Busy = busy (English word used in Kannada). Great small talk phrase to start a chat.

questions.prompt: It's been raining and you want to make small talk about the weather.
questions.explanation: Tumba male = lots of rain. Aagutte = is happening/will be. Sari aagutte = it's good / it's fine. 'Lots of rain, that's good' — locals love saying this in summer.

questions.prompt: The chai wala says 'Nimdu regular spot idu, yaavaglu barri'. What is he saying?

options.text: This is your regular spot, come anytime
Your spot is taken, come back later

questions.explanation: Nimdu = yours. Regular spot = regular spot. Yaavaglu = anytime/always. Barri = come (polite). A warm invitation to become a regular — this is local hospitality.

questions.prompt: You want to compliment the chai: 'Today's chai is very good'. Complete: 'Indu chai tumba ___'
questions.hint: chenna aagutte = is/has become good (used as a compliment)

title: Kirana Store
description: Buy groceries, ask for items, and become a regular

questions.prompt: You want to ask 'Do you have coconut oil?'
questions.explanation: Tengina = coconut. Enne = oil. Ide-aa? = is it there? The -aa at the end makes it a yes/no question. Ask first before ordering.

questions.prompt: You ask for something and the shopkeeper says 'Stock aagitta, naale baratte'. What does he mean?

options.text: Stock is finished, it'll come tomorrow
New stock arrived today, come back later
This item is only available tomorrow

questions.explanation: Stock aagitta = stock is done/over (aagitta = has become/is done). Naale = tomorrow. Baratte = it will come. He's telling you to come back tomorrow.

questions.prompt: You need a packet of salt and a kilo of rice.

options.text: Ondu uppu packet, akki ondu kilo kodi

questions.explanation: Uppu = salt. Akki = rice. Ondu = one. Kodi = give. List items in order and end with kodi — that's all you need.

questions.prompt: You want a specific brand but they offer a substitute. You want to say 'No, only that brand'.
questions.explanation: Illa = no. Aa = that. Maatrame = only. Beka = I want/I need. Aa brand maatrame beka = I need only that brand. Clear and direct.

questions.prompt: The shopkeeper says 'Cash illa-aa? Gpay maadi'. What does he want?

options.text: Don't have enough cash, use GPay for extra

questions.explanation: Cash illa-aa? = no cash? GPay maadi = do GPay. Very common at Bangalore kirana stores — most now prefer UPI. Maadi = do (respectful command).

questions.prompt: You want to put groceries on credit (khata). Complete: '___ haakodiri'
questions.hint: Khata = credit account. Khata-ge = to the khata/account. Haakodiri = please put/add (respectful).

questions.prompt: You want 250 grams of cumin seeds.
questions.explanation: Jeerige = cumin seeds. Kaalu kilo = quarter kilo (250g). Kaalu = quarter (1/4). Ardha = half (500g). Ondu = full one kilo.

questions.prompt: The shopkeeper says 'Loose ide-aa, packet-nalli bekaa?'. What is he asking?

options.text: Do you want it loose or in a packet?
Is it loose in a packet already?
The packet is loose, should I tighten it?

questions.explanation: Loose ide = it's loose/unpackaged. Packet-nalli = in a packet. Bekaa? = do you want/need? He's asking if you want it weighed loose or pre-packaged — loose is usually cheaper.

questions.prompt: The scale shows 480g but you asked for 500g. You say:
questions.explanation: Swalpa kamma = a little less. Aagutte = it is. 500g beka = I need 500g. Pointing to the scale while saying this makes it very clear.

questions.prompt: You want to ask 'Is this full weight?'
questions.explanation: Tookka = weight (in the sense of measured weight). Sari = correct/right. Ide-aa? = is it? Tookka sari ide-aa? = Is the weight correct? Useful when you're suspicious of the scale.

questions.prompt: The shopkeeper gives you a little extra and says 'Ondu kaalu jaasti'. What did he add?
questions.explanation: Ondu kaalu = one quarter. Jaasti = extra/more. So ondu kaalu jaasti = one quarter extra. This is a generous gesture from a friendly shopkeeper.

questions.prompt: You want 'a little' of something. Complete: 'Swalpa ___ kodi' (give me a little turmeric)
questions.hint: arishina = turmeric. A bright yellow spice used in almost every Karnataka dish.

questions.prompt: You're shopping for the first time at a new kirana. You want to introduce yourself as a local.

options.text: Naanu hattira-ve iddhene, nimage regular aagutte

questions.explanation: Hattira-ve = right nearby. Iddhene = I am/I live. Nimage = to you. Regular aagutte = will become a regular. 'I live right nearby, I'll be a regular' — shopkeepers love this.

questions.prompt: The shopkeeper says 'Nimge home delivery maaduttene'. What is he offering?
questions.explanation: Nimge = for you / to you (formal). Home delivery maaduttene = I'll do/give home delivery. Many Bangalore kirana stores offer free delivery to regulars — great to know.

questions.prompt: You want to say 'Please keep this aside for me'.
questions.explanation: Naange = for me. Aachege = aside / set apart. Idri = please keep (respectful). 'Please keep it set aside for me' — great for reserving something before paying.

questions.prompt: At the end of the month you want to settle your credit account. You say:

options.text: Khata tumba aagutte, indu clear maadona

questions.explanation: Khata tumba aagutte = the account has gotten big. Clear maadona = let's clear it. Indu = today. A natural way to initiate settling your tab.

questions.prompt: The shopkeeper says 'Nimma khata-nalli 450 ide'. What does he mean?

options.text: You have 450 rupees on your credit account
You have 450 rupees in credit (he owes you)

questions.explanation: Nimma = your. Khata-nalli = in the account. 450 ide = there is 450. He's telling you your outstanding balance. Pay up!

questions.prompt: You forgot something. Complete: 'Ondu nimishe, ___ marete' (Wait a moment, I forgot something)
questions.hint: enu-o = something (indefinite). Marete = I forgot. 'Something I forgot.'

title: Neighbors & Daily Life
description: Build real relationships with the people around you

questions.prompt: You see your neighbor on the way out in the morning. The natural greeting is:
questions.explanation: Hoguttiddira? = are you going? (present continuous, polite). Seeing someone leaving, asking if they're heading out is a natural opener. Baruttiddira = are you coming? — wrong if they're clearly leaving.

questions.prompt: Your neighbor says 'Swalpa kelsa ide, office-ge hoguttiddene'. What are they saying?

options.text: Have a little work, going to the office
Coming back from the office, some work pending
The office has a lot of work today

questions.explanation: Swalpa = a little. Kelsa = work. Ide = there is. Office-ge = to the office. Hoguttiddene = I am going. A casual response when you're in a hurry.

questions.prompt: You want to say 'My name is Rahul, I live on the second floor'.

options.text: Nanna hesaru Rahul, eradu maalige-nalli iddhene
Naanu Rahul, eradu angadi hattira iddhene

questions.explanation: Nanna hesaru = my name. Eradu = two/second. Maalige = floor/storey. Nalli = in. Iddhene = I am/I live. Very useful for introducing yourself to a new neighbor.

questions.prompt: It's been a few days since you've seen your neighbor. A warm way to say 'Haven't seen you in a while':
questions.explanation: Swalpa = little/few. Dina = days. Nalli = in. Kaanenilla = I didn't see. 'Didn't see you for a few days' — warm without being intrusive.

questions.prompt: Your neighbor says 'Ooru hogiddhe, nannu bandhe'. What do they mean?

options.text: Went to my hometown, just came back
Going to my hometown, I'll come back
Came from my hometown, going back tomorrow

questions.explanation: Ooru = hometown/native place (very important word in Bangalore). Hogiddhe = I had gone. Nannu = just now. Bandhe = I came. 'Had gone to native, just returned' — explains an absence.

questions.prompt: You want to ask 'When did you come back?' Complete: 'Yaavaaga ___?'
questions.hint: banddhira = did you come? (past tense question, formal). yaavaaga = when

questions.prompt: You're locked out and want to ask your neighbor if you can use their phone.
questions.explanation: Nimma = your. Phone use maadabahudu-aa? = Can I use the phone? Bahudu = may/can (polite permission). Kodi = give me — too direct here. Maadabahudu-aa is the right form for asking permission.

questions.prompt: You ask your neighbor for a favor and they say 'Yaavude problem illa, maadi'. What do they mean?

options.text: No problem at all, go ahead / I'll do it
There's a small problem, I'll fix it

questions.explanation: Yaavude = any/whatever. Problem illa = no problem. Maadi = do it/go ahead. 'Yaavude problem illa' is a genuinely warm 'absolutely no problem' in Kannada.

questions.prompt: There's been a power cut and you want to ask if their building has power.
questions.explanation: Nimma = your. Building-nalli = in the building. Current = electricity (universally used in Bangalore). Ide-aa? = is there? 'Current' not 'electricity' is what locals say.

questions.prompt: Your neighbor helped you and you want to say 'Thank you very much, you saved me'.
questions.explanation: Tumba = very. Dhanyavaada = thank you. Ulisiddhira = you saved (me). Naannu = me. A heartfelt thank-you. Ulisiddhira is used both literally (saved) and figuratively (you were a lifesaver).

questions.prompt: Your neighbor says 'Bere yaavude sahaya beka aadare heli'. What are they offering?

options.text: If you need any other help, just ask
You can help me with something else
That help was not necessary, no need

questions.explanation: Bere = other/else. Yaavude = any. Sahaya = help. Beka aadare = if you need. Heli = tell me/ask. 'If you need any other help, just tell me' — warm neighborly offer.

questions.prompt: You want to say 'I'll definitely return the favor'. Complete: 'Naanu ___ madtane iddene'
questions.hint: mathe = again / in return. madtane = will definitely do. 'I will definitely do it in return.'

questions.prompt: The watchman sees you late at night and wants to know where you're going. A friendly response:

options.text: Swalpa kaafi kudiyakke hoguttiddhene, bayage baruttene

questions.explanation: Swalpa kaafi kudiyakke = to drink a little coffee. Bayage = outside. Baruttene = I'll come back. A warm, transparent answer builds trust with the watchman. 'Neevu yaake keLtira?' = why are you asking? — too defensive.

questions.prompt: The house help says 'Indu baralla, naale baruttene'. What should you expect?

options.text: Not coming today, will come tomorrow

questions.explanation: Indu = today. Baralla = will not come. Naale = tomorrow. Baruttene = will come. Critical phrase to recognize so you can plan your day accordingly!

questions.prompt: You want to tell the plumber 'The tap is leaking, please fix it'.

options.text: Tap leaka aagutte, sari maadi kodi

questions.explanation: Tap leaka aagutte = the tap is leaking. Sari maadi kodi = please fix / please set right. Sari maadu = to fix/correct. Works for most repair requests.

questions.prompt: You want to give your neighbor your phone number so they can call in an emergency.

options.text: Nanna number ittukoli, yaavude vishaya-nalli call maadi
Nimma number kodi, naanu call maaduttene

questions.explanation: Nanna = my. Ittukoli = keep it (save it). Yaavude = any. Vishaya = matter/thing. Naanu call maadi = call me. 'Keep my number, call for anything' — great for building local community.

questions.prompt: A neighbor says 'Nimge Kannada tumba chenna baratte'. What are they saying?

options.text: Your Kannada is coming along very nicely
Your Kannada is too difficult to understand

questions.explanation: Nimge = to you / your. Tumba = very. Chenna = good/nicely. Baratte = it comes / you speak. A wonderful compliment you'll hear once you start using these phrases!

questions.prompt: You want to say 'I am learning, slowly slowly'. Complete: 'Naanu kaliyuttiddhene, ___ ___'
questions.hint: nidhaanav = slowly. Repeating it ('slowly slowly') is natural emphasis in Kannada.

title: Getting Around
description: Navigate the city — buses, directions, and local landmarks

questions.prompt: You want to ask 'Where is the bus stop?'
questions.explanation: Elli = where. Ide? = is there? Elli ide? is the core 'where is' question. Works for anything: 'Hospital elli ide?' 'ATM elli ide?'

questions.prompt: Someone says 'Nere hogi, signal aadmele edakke tiri'. Where do you end up?

options.text: Go straight, then turn left after the signal
Turn left at the signal, then go straight
Go straight past the signal, then right

questions.explanation: Nere hogi = go straight. Signal aadmele = after the signal passes. Edakke = left. Tiri = turn. Aadmele is a very useful word meaning 'after' or 'once that's done'.

questions.prompt: You've been walking and think you're lost. You stop someone and ask:
questions.explanation: Elli aagutte? = where will it be? / where is it? Used when asking about a general area. 'Illi ide?' would mean 'is it right here?' — too specific when you're lost.

questions.prompt: Someone says 'Swalpa dooradalli ide, naadekondu hogbahadu'. What are they telling you?

options.text: It's a little far, you can walk there
It's nearby but the road is confusing

questions.explanation: Swalpa dooradalli = a little far. Naadekondu = walking. Hogbahadu = you can go. 'It's a little far, you can walk' — an honest answer. Decide if you want to walk or take an auto.

questions.prompt: You want to ask 'How far is it from here?'
questions.explanation: Illiinda = from here. Inda = from. Eshtu = how much. Dura = far/distance. Ide? = is it? Illiinda eshtu dura ide? = How far is it from here?

questions.prompt: You want to say 'I don't know this area'. Complete: 'Naange ee ___ gottilla'
questions.hint: jaaga = place/area/location. Gottilla = I don't know.

questions.prompt: You want to ask 'Does this bus go to Majestic?'
questions.explanation: Ee = this. Hoguttaa? = does it go? (question form of hoguttide). Ge = to. This works on BMTC — just point at the bus and ask.

questions.prompt: You're on the bus. You want to tell the conductor where you're going to get a ticket.
questions.explanation: On Bangalore buses, just say the destination + 'ondu' (one). The conductor knows you want one ticket. No need for 'ticket kodi' or full sentences.

questions.prompt: The conductor says 'Nimage yaavudu stop beku?'. What does he want to know?

options.text: Did you get off at the wrong stop?
Is this your first time on the bus?

questions.explanation: Nimage = for you / which do you want. Yaavudu = which. Stop = stop. Beku = want/need. He's asking your destination stop — common when you look confused.

questions.prompt: You want to ask 'When will the next bus come?'
questions.explanation: Munde = next/ahead. Bus = bus. Yaavaaga = when. Barutte = will come. Munde bus yaavaaga barutte? = When will the next bus come? Ask this at any BMTC stop.

questions.prompt: Your stop is coming up. You want to signal to get off.
questions.explanation: Illi = here. BiDri = let me off / drop here (request for the conductor). Barri = come here. Nilli = stop (for a vehicle). biDri is specifically the phrase for 'let me get off here'.

questions.prompt: You missed your stop. Complete: 'Nanna stop ___ aagutte' (My stop has passed / I missed my stop)
questions.hint: hinde = behind/back. hinde aagutte = has gone behind = I've passed it.

questions.prompt: Someone tells you 'Aa doddada mara hattira tiri'. Where should you turn?
questions.explanation: Aa = that. Doddadu = big/large. Mara = tree. Hattira = near. Tiri = turn. Locals often give directions using trees, shops, and landmarks rather than street names.

questions.prompt: You're trying to describe your house location. A local-sounding description would be:
questions.explanation: Hinde = behind. Kempada = red-colored. Building-nalli = in the building. 'Behind D-Mart, in the red building' — this is exactly how locals give addresses. Landmarks over street names always.

questions.prompt: You want to ask 'Is there an ATM nearby?'
questions.explanation: Hattira = nearby/close. ATM = ATM. Ide-aa? = is there? Hattira ATM ide-aa? = Is there an ATM nearby? Works for any shop or facility — just swap 'ATM' for what you need.

questions.prompt: Someone says 'Illi ondu roundabout ide, adara nantara balaakke tiri'. What do you do?

options.text: There's a roundabout here, turn right after it
Go around the roundabout and go straight

questions.explanation: Ondu = one. Roundabout ide = there is a roundabout. Adara nantara = after that. Balaakke = right. Tiri = turn. Nantara is an important word meaning 'after that'.

questions.prompt: You're completely lost. The best thing to say to get real help:

options.text: Naanu illi hosa, jaaga gottilla — swalpa help maadi

questions.explanation: Naanu illi hosa = I am new here. Jaaga gottilla = I don't know this place. Swalpa help maadi = please help a little. Admitting you're new gets you genuine local help every time.
